messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kareem Haddad is a 41-year-old single Lebanese-American construction worker who presented for his first psychological consultation after what he described, with visible reluctance, as "finally running out of other options." He has spent the better part of three decades managing the aftermath of what he witnessed as a child, and it is only now, with his functioning visibly narrowing, that he has allowed himself to sit in a therapist's office and attempt to account for it.

Kareem grew up in a household in Dearborn, Michigan, in which his father's rages were a recurring and unpredictable feature of domestic life. The violence he witnessed was not occasional — it was cyclical and escalating. What lodged most deeply in Kareem's memory, however, was a specific night when he was approximately nine years old. His father had come home late, and Kareem had been in the hallway when the argument began. He remembers with photographic precision the way his mother's back was pressed against the kitchen wall, the overhead light flickering, the particular angle of his father's raised arm. Other moments from that night are simply gone — blank spaces where memory should be — and when Kareem tries to deliberately reconstruct the sequence of events, he finds himself unable to access them in any ordered way. The images arrive not as narrative but as stills: isolated, vivid, and stripped of context. What he cannot retrieve deliberately arrives unbidden at other times, uninvited and complete.

In the years that followed, Kareem learned to read rooms. He became extraordinarily attentive to the faces of the men around him — foremen, co-workers, strangers on job sites — scanning for the particular tightening around the jaw, the shift in posture, the quality of stillness that in his childhood had preceded violence. On a construction site this vigilance is constant, and it exhausts him. When a delivery runs late or a subcontractor fails to show on schedule, Kareem does not interpret the delay as logistical — he is certain, in those moments, that something has gone wrong in a more fundamental sense, that the silence before the disruption is the same silence he once stood in at the end of that hallway. His body responds accordingly: his chest tightens, his hands become unsteady, and he has on several occasions had to remove himself from the work floor without explanation.

He avoids confrontation with a discipline that has shaped his entire social world. When disputes arise on site — over materials, timelines, or the ordinary friction of men working in close quarters — Kareem goes quiet and withdraws. He has turned down two supervisory positions over the past six years because he understood, correctly, that the role would require him to manage conflict directly. When police officers appear near a job site, as they occasionally do in the neighbourhoods where he works, he experiences an acute physical response and finds reasons to position himself elsewhere until they leave. He has come to believe that his body simply cannot tolerate the presence of authority in uniform without treating it as a precursor to harm.

In the evenings, Kareem drifts. He describes it as going somewhere else — a private interior space that is neither sleep nor fantasy exactly, but a retreat from the present into something quieter. He also finds himself dwelling on who he was before the weight of all this became so apparent to him: a younger version of himself who laughed more easily, who had been briefly engaged in his early thirties before the relationship ended under the strain of his withdrawal. He does not talk about the future with any ease. When a colleague recently asked him what he planned to do when the current project wrapped up, Kareem felt his throat close. The future, he has come to feel, is not a place he can safely imagine occupying.

What brought him in, finally, was a moment on site last month when a foreman raised his voice during a scheduling dispute. Kareem did not respond. He walked to his truck and sat there for forty minutes, shaking, unable to account for himself to anyone, including himself. He is hoping, he said carefully, to understand why a grown man is still standing in that hallway.
